505.title: Many names for a bowl
505.hook: don't insist on your local word; a bowl has many names
505.howItsDone: Buddhist teachings are chanted and studied in many languages, including Pali, Sanskrit, Chinese, Tibetan, Japanese and today English, and the Vinaya records the Buddha allowing monks to learn the teaching in their own dialect.

segments.voice: Yesterday: forty tabs and a pleasant fog, and your line, not scattered, not stuck. Did you close one tab and step out of one thought? Today, a new week, and a bowl. Day five hundred five.

Soda. Pop. Coke, even when it isn't. Sneakers or tennis shoes. Some people have argued about these words at a family reunion with real heat. The hundred and thirty-ninth discourse is about living without conflict, and most of it is about big things: pleasure and self-torment, praise and blame, how to speak. But tucked inside is a small, almost funny example about tableware. The Buddha notices that the same simple bowl goes by different names in different districts. And he has something to say about people who insist theirs is the real one. Today: many names for a bowl.
screen: `SODA. POP. COKE.` → `A DISCOURSE ON NON-CONFLICT.` → `ONE BOWL, MANY NAMES.`

segments.voice: The discourse is called the exposition of non-conflict, araṇa. It gives a list of ways to live without stirring up conflict. Don't pursue sensual pleasure, and don't torment yourself: the middle way. Know what praise and blame are, and teach without either. Don't say things in secret that would hurt if known, or speak harshly to someone's face. Speak unhurriedly, because hurried speech tires the body and the mind, and is hard to follow. And then: don't insist on local language, and don't override ordinary usage. Here's the example. In one district, the Buddha says, people call a bowl pati. In another, patta. In others, by still other names. Someone who clings to their own district's word says: only this is correct, everything else is wrong. That person, the text says, is insisting on local language and overriding ordinary usage, and that's a path with conflict in it. The other person, wherever they go, thinks: it seems these people call it this. And speaks as they do, without grasping. That's the path without conflict. It's remarkable that a teaching about freedom stops to talk about kitchen words. But it fits. Many fights aren't about the thing. They're about whose name for it wins. In the monastic rules, many readers find the Buddha letting monks learn his words in their own dialects, and the teaching did travel far that way. A bowl holds rice whatever it's called. The text ends by naming a monk, Subhuti, as one who walked this way of non-conflict.
screen: `ARANA: THE WAY OF NON-CONFLICT` · `SPEAK UNHURRIEDLY` · `PATI, PATTA, AND MORE` · `SPEAK AS THEY DO` · then, large: `MANY NAMES FOR A BOWL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: allow one other word. Sit and settle. Think of a word, a name, a way of saying something that you've corrected someone about, or wanted to. Maybe a term for God, a holiday, a dish, a pronunciation. Picture them saying it their way. Notice any little push to fix it. Then let the push soften: it seems they call it this. Let the breath be unhurried. The bell holds the time.
Many names for a bowl. Pati, patta and more: don't insist your local word is the only right one; speak as people speak, without grasping. Today's word.
screen: `MANY NAMES FOR A BOWL — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: many names for a bowl. Today, when someone uses a different word than you would, let it stand, and try using theirs once. Day five hundred five.

screen: `DAY 505 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE STRANGER WAS THE TEACHER.`

what it means: many conflicts are about whose word wins; the Buddha's way is to speak as others speak, without grasping.

506.title: The stranger was the teacher
506.hook: Pukkusati meets the Buddha in a potter's shed without knowing him, and is taught the six elements
506.howItsDone: The six-element contemplation of MN 140 is taught in Theravada and other meditation traditions, with practitioners reviewing earth, water, fire, air, space and consciousness in the body and seeing each as not-self.

segments.voice: Yesterday: pati and patta, and your line, many names for a bowl. Did you try someone else's word once? Today, a stranger in a potter's shed. Day five hundred six.

Evening, on the road near Rajagaha. A wandering monk asks a potter named Bhaggava if he can spend the night in his workshop. The potter says: fine by me, but someone's already staying there. Ask him. Inside is a young man who has shaved his head and left home out of faith in a teacher he has never met. His name is Pukkusati. The traveler asks: may I stay? Pukkusati says: the workshop is roomy. Stay as you like. He has no idea who just walked in. Today: the stranger was the teacher.
screen: `A POTTER'S WORKSHOP AT EVENING.` → `PUKKUSATI, FAITHFUL, NEVER MET HIM.` → `A TRAVELER ASKS TO STAY.`

segments.voice: They sit through most of the night. Then the traveler asks: on whose account did you go forth? Who's your teacher? Pukkusati answers: the recluse Gotama, the Sakyan. I went forth because of him. Have you seen him? asks the traveler. Would you recognize him? No, says Pukkusati. I've never seen him. If I saw him, I wouldn't know him. The Buddha doesn't reveal himself. He thinks: this young man went forth on my account. Let me teach him. And he does. A person, he says, is made of six elements: earth, water, fire, air, space and consciousness. He takes each one: the solid in the body is earth, and so is the solid outside it. Seeing that, you see: this is not mine, this is not me, this is not my self. Same for water, fire, air and space. Then what remains is consciousness, and then a pure, bright equanimity, like gold refined by a goldsmith until it's soft and shining. And even that, he says, is conditioned, and he shows how to let go of it too. Partway through, Pukkusati understands who's speaking. He bows and asks forgiveness for calling the Buddha friend, like an equal. The Buddha accepts. Pukkusati asks for full ordination, and is told he needs a bowl and robes. He goes to find them. And on the way, the text says, a stray cow kills him. The Buddha tells the monks Pukkusati had already gone far, beyond returning to this world. He had found his teacher, for one night, without knowing it.
screen: `HAVE YOU SEEN HIM?` · `SIX ELEMENTS: NOT MINE, NOT ME` · `GOLD REFINED TO SHINING` · `HE KNOWS, AND BOWS` · then, large: `THE STRANGER WAS THE TEACHER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn from a stranger. Sit and settle. Feel the solid in you: earth. The moist: water. The warmth: fire. The breath moving: air. The spaces in mouth and ears: space. And knowing it all: consciousness. Then think of someone you'll meet today whom you don't really know, a cashier, a driver, a new colleague. Leave a little room for the possibility that they have something to teach you. The bell holds the time.
The stranger was the teacher. Pukkusati spent a night in a potter's shed with the Buddha, not knowing him, and was taught the six elements. Today's word.
screen: `THE STRANGER WAS THE TEACHER — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the stranger was the teacher. Today, ask one person you don't know well a real question, and listen as if they might be the one. Day five hundred six.

options: tell him at once who you are.
teach him, and let him discover it.

fork.reveal: the Buddha teaches him the six elements first; Pukkusati recognizes him through the teaching itself.

original.note: Pali dhatu: element. MN 140 teaches six: earth, water, fire, air, space and consciousness.

trapdoor: what you thought: you'd know your teacher if you met them.
what it means: Pukkusati found his teacher through the teaching, before he knew the face.

what a scholar hears: MN 140, the Dhatuvibhanga Sutta, combines the six-element analysis with the goldsmith simile; the commentary adds that Pukkusati was a king of Takkasila who renounced after hearing of the Buddha.

507.title: The truths expounded
507.hook: Sariputta sets out the four truths in detail
507.howItsDone: Buddhists across traditions learn the four noble truths as the core of the teaching, and Theravada monastics often study detailed expositions like MN 141 and its parallel in the Digha Nikaya's discourse on the foundations of mindfulness.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Pukkusati in the potter's shed, and your line, the stranger was the teacher. Did you ask someone a real question? Today, back where it all began. Day five hundred seven.

The hundred and forty-first discourse is set at the Deer Park at Isipatana, near Benares, the same place where, in the tradition, the Buddha first taught the four noble truths to five companions. Years later, he's there again. He reminds the monks that the wheel of the teaching was first set rolling right here, by announcing four truths. Then he does something a good teacher does. He points to two students. Go to Sariputta and Moggallana, he says. Learn from them. And he goes into his dwelling. Today: the truths expounded.
screen: `THE DEER PARK, NEAR BENARES.` → `WHERE THE WHEEL FIRST ROLLED.` → `GO TO SARIPUTTA AND MOGGALLANA.`

segments.voice: Before he leaves, the Buddha gives a picture of his two chief students. Sariputta, he says, is like a mother who gives birth. Moggallana is like a nurse who raises the child. Sariputta trains people to the first real breakthrough. Moggallana trains them to the highest goal. So Sariputta stands up and does what the title says: he expounds. He takes each truth and opens it. First, suffering. Birth is suffering, he says, and then defines birth, the coming into being of beings. Aging is suffering, and he defines aging: gray hair, wrinkled skin, failing faculties. Death, sorrow, grief, despair, each one named and described. Not getting what you want is suffering. And in short, the five heaps that are clung to are suffering. Second, the origin: craving that leads to renewed being, craving for pleasure, for becoming, for non-becoming. Third, the cessation: the complete fading and ending of that craving, letting it go. Fourth, the path: and here he defines each of the eight factors one by one, from right view, knowing these four truths, to right concentration. Nothing dramatic happens. No one is suddenly freed in the story. It's a careful lecture, almost a textbook. And that's the point. The four truths can be announced in a minute, as the Buddha did at the start. But they're meant to be unfolded, slowly, word by word, by students who've learned them well enough to teach. Expounded means laid out, line by line, so others can walk through it.
screen: `A MOTHER AND A NURSE` · `SUFFERING, DEFINED WORD BY WORD` · `CRAVING, ITS ENDING, THE PATH` · `ANNOUNCED, THEN UNFOLDED` · then, large: `EXPOUNDED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: recite the four truths. Sit and settle. In your own words, slowly, one with each out-breath. There is suffering. It has a cause: craving. It can end. There is a path. Then go around again, and this time let each line touch something real from your week, a small ache, a want, a moment of ease, a step you took. The bell holds the time.
The truths expounded. At the Deer Park, Sariputta lays out the four noble truths in detail, defining each one word by word. Today's word.
Your line: expounded. Today, take one idea you think you know and explain it slowly to someone, or to yourself, word by word. Day five hundred seven.

fork.reveal: Sariputta is the mother, training people to the first breakthrough; Moggallana the nurse, training them to the highest goal.

trapdoor: what you thought: the four noble truths are four short slogans.

what a scholar hears: MN 141, the Saccavibhanga Sutta, gives a detailed analysis closely paralleled in the Mahasatipatthana Sutta (DN 22), and frames Sariputta and Moggallana's complementary roles.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 141, Saccavibhanga Sutta (the exposition of the truths)

508.title: The robe gift
508.hook: Mahapajapati offers a robe she made; the kinds of offering
508.howItsDone: In Theravada countries the Kathina ceremony at the end of the rains retreat is a major occasion when lay people offer robe cloth to the monastic community as a whole, rather than to one monk.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the mother and the nurse, and your line, expounded. Did you explain one idea slowly? Today, the woman who raised the Buddha brings him a gift. Day five hundred eight.

A sweater someone knitted for you. It took them weeks. It's a little lopsided, and you'd never give it away. The hundred and forty-second discourse begins with a gift like that. The Buddha is back home among the Sakyans, at Kapilavatthu. Mahapajapati Gotami, his mother's sister, the woman who raised him after his mother died, comes to him with a new robe cloth. She spun the thread herself. She wove it herself. She says: this is for you, Lord. Please accept it out of compassion. And the Buddha says no. Today: the robe gift.
screen: `A HAND-KNITTED SWEATER.` → `SPUN AND WOVEN BY HER OWN HANDS.` → `THE BUDDHA SAYS: GIVE IT TO THE SANGHA.`

segments.voice: Give it to the community, Gotami, the Buddha says. When you give to the community, both I and the community are honored. She asks again. He says the same thing. A third time. Then Ananda steps in, gently. Lord, please accept it. She was so helpful to you. She was your mother's sister, your nurse, your foster mother. When your mother died, she gave you her own milk. And the Buddha has helped her too, Ananda adds: through him she found refuge and the precepts. The Buddha agrees that each has helped the other, and that such debts can't be easily repaid with robes or food. Then he turns the moment into a teaching about giving. He lists fourteen kinds of personal gifts, from a gift to a Buddha down to a gift to an animal. Even a gift to an animal, he says, can be expected to repay a hundredfold. Then seven kinds of gifts to the community. And then four ways a gift is made pure: by the giver, by the receiver, by both, or by neither, depending on whose conduct is good. Why refuse his foster mother? The discourse doesn't explain in a single line, and it doesn't say what happened to the robe. One common reading: he wanted her gift to reach as many people as it could, and to grow her merit beyond one person. A later commentary tells its own story of where the robe went. What's clear is the gift itself: thread spun by hand, for someone loved, and a teaching about generosity that grew from it.
screen: `GIVE IT TO THE COMMUNITY` · `ANANDA: SHE NURSED YOU` · `FOURTEEN GIFTS, FOUR PURITIES` · `A GIFT MADE TO REACH FAR` · then, large: `MADE BY HAND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give something handmade. Sit and settle. Think of someone you could give a small thing made by your own hands: a note written out, not typed; a meal; a drawing; a repaired thing. Picture making it. Notice the care that goes in before anyone receives it. That's part of the gift too. Then rest with the breath, and if you like, let the idea grow into a plan. The bell holds the time.
The robe gift. Mahapajapati's handmade robe, which the Buddha asked her to give to the whole community, and the teaching on giving that followed. Today's word.
Your line: made by hand. Today, make one small thing for someone, a note, a snack, a fixed button, and give it without fuss. Day five hundred eight.

original.note: Pali dakkhina: an offering, a gift given with respect. MN 142 is the exposition of offerings.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Buddha refused his mother's gift.
what it means: he asked that her handmade gift go to the whole community, and taught how giving bears fruit.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 142, Dakkhinavibhanga Sutta (the exposition of offerings)

509.title: Anathapindika's last days
509.hook: dying, the great giver is taught not to cling to anything, and weeps at its depth
509.howItsDone: In many Buddhist communities monks or friends visit the dying to chant and to recall teachings on non-clinging, and MN 143 is one of the discourses sometimes read at a deathbed.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Mahapajapati's robe, and your line, made by hand. Did you make one small thing for someone? Today, another great giver, near the end. Day five hundred nine.

Anathapindika's name means the one who gives food to the unprotected. He's the merchant who, in the tradition, bought Jeta's Grove for the Buddha by covering the ground with coins. Half the discourses you've heard this year happened in the park he gave. Now he is very ill. He sends a messenger to the Buddha with his respects, and another to Sariputta: please come, out of compassion. Sariputta comes, with Ananda. He asks how Anathapindika is. And the answer is honest: the pain is getting worse, not better. Today: Anathapindika's last days.
screen: `THE ONE WHO FEEDS THE UNPROTECTED.` → `THE GIVER OF JETA'S GROVE.` → `THE PAIN IS GETTING WORSE.`

segments.voice: He describes it plainly, in the text's images: like a strong man splitting his head with a sharp sword, like a tight strap around the head, like a butcher's knife in the belly, like being held over hot coals. Sariputta doesn't offer comfort first. He offers a training. You should train like this, householder, he says. I won't cling to the eye, and my consciousness won't depend on the eye. I won't cling to the ear. The nose, the tongue, the body, the mind. I won't cling to sights, sounds, smells, tastes, touches or thoughts. Not to the elements, not to the five heaps. Not to this world, and my consciousness won't depend on this world. Not to any world beyond. Not to anything seen, heard, sensed, known, sought or explored. Line after line, everything a dying person might hold. And Anathapindika weeps. Ananda asks: are you sinking, householder? No, he says. I've served the Teacher and the monks for so long, and I've never heard a talk like this. Sariputta answers that such talks are usually given to monastics, not to lay people. And Anathapindika, almost with his last breath, asks for something. Let talks like this be given to lay people too. There are those with little dust in their eyes who will be lost if they never hear it. Soon after they leave, he dies. The text says he was reborn among the gods, and came back one night to Jeta's Grove, glowing, to praise it and Sariputta. The great giver's last gift was a request: share this with everyone.
screen: `PAIN LIKE A SWORD, A STRAP, COALS` · `I WON'T CLING TO THIS` · `HE WEEPS: I'VE NEVER HEARD THIS` · `LET LAY PEOPLE HEAR IT TOO` · then, large: `NOT CLINGING TO THIS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let go of one thing. Sit and settle. Choose one small thing you're holding today: a plan, an opinion, a worry about tomorrow, a feeling about yourself. Breathing in, notice how you hold it. Breathing out, say quietly, in Sariputta's spirit: not clinging to this. You don't have to throw it away. Just loosen the grip for one breath, then another. The bell holds the time.
Anathapindika's last days. Dying, the great giver hears Sariputta teach not clinging to anything at all, weeps at its depth, and asks that lay people hear it too. Today's word.
Your line: not clinging to this. Today, when you feel yourself gripping something, say the line once and loosen your hands. Day five hundred nine.

fork.reveal: Sariputta teaches non-clinging, line by line, from the eye to every world. Anathapindika weeps at its depth.

trapdoor: what you thought: at a deathbed, you comfort someone.

510.title: Punna goes west
510.hook: to a fierce land: if they insult me, I'll think them kind for not hitting me
510.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often tell Punna's story to illustrate patience (khanti), one of the perfections, and monastics who move to new regions to teach are sometimes compared to him.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Anathapindika's last request, and your line, not clinging to this. Did you loosen your grip once? Today, a monk heading somewhere hard. Day five hundred ten.

A new job, a new city, a team with a reputation. Everyone warns you: they're rough over there. You'll get eaten alive. The hundred and forty-fifth discourse starts with a monk named Punna asking the Buddha for a short teaching before he leaves. The Buddha gives it, then asks: where will you live? Punna names a region to the west called Sunaparanta. The Buddha says, plainly: the people there are fierce, Punna. They're rough. What will you do if they insult you? Today: Punna goes west.
screen: `THEY'RE ROUGH OVER THERE.` → `PUNNA NAMES THE WEST.` → `WHAT IF THEY INSULT YOU?`

segments.voice: The short teaching comes first. If you delight in what you see, hear, smell, taste, touch and think, and hold on to it, suffering comes. If you don't, it ends. Then the conversation, and it's like a ladder going down. If they insult you? Punna: I'll think, these people are good, really good, since they don't hit me with their fists. And if they hit you with their fists? I'll think, they're good, since they don't throw clods of earth at me. And if they do? At least they don't beat me with a stick. And if they do? At least they don't use a knife. The Buddha keeps going, all the way to the worst, and Punna's answer never turns to hate. Even facing the end of his life, he answers calmly. The Buddha says: good, Punna. With such self-control and peace, you can live there. Punna goes. The text says that in that one rains retreat he brought around five hundred men and five hundred women as lay followers, realized the three knowledges, and later attained final release. A word of care, though. This is a monk's training in patience, chosen freely, in a teaching about not clinging. It isn't advice to stay where someone hurts you. What anyone can borrow is the move itself: when something sharp lands, notice what didn't happen. They were rude, but they didn't shout. The email was curt, but it wasn't cruel. That's not pretending it was fine. It's refusing to let the worst version take over the mind. At least they didn't.
screen: `DELIGHT AND HOLDING BRING SUFFERING` · `INSULT, FIST, CLOD, STICK` · `NEVER TURNING TO HATE` · `NOT ADVICE TO STAY IN HARM` · then, large: `AT LEAST THEY DIDN'T.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: reframe one insult. Sit and settle. Bring to mind a small sting from recently: a curt reply, an eye-roll, a comment that landed. Not a deep wound, just a small one. Notice how it sits in the body. Then try Punna's step: what didn't happen? They were short with me, but they didn't. Let the sting be its real size, no bigger. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Punna goes west. A monk heading to a fierce land answers every imagined harm without hatred: at least they didn't do worse. Today's word.
Your line: at least they didn't. Today, when a small rudeness lands, name one thing it wasn't, and let it stay small. Day five hundred ten.

it's a monk's freely chosen training in patience, not a rule for anyone being hurt.

original.note: Pali khanti: patience, forbearance. Punna's answers are often taught as an example of it.

trapdoor: what you thought: Punna is just being a pushover.
what it means: he trains the mind not to inflate harm or turn to hatred, after a teaching on not clinging.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 145, Punnovada Sutta (advice to Punna)

511.title: Nandaka's full moon
511.hook: an elder teaches the nuns; they are satisfied like the full moon
511.howItsDone: In Theravada monastic rules, bhikkhunis receive regular instruction (ovada) from a qualified bhikkhu, often on the observance day, and teachers commonly use the question-and-answer method of discourses like MN 146.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Punna's ladder, and your line, at least they didn't. Did a small rudeness stay small? Today closes a week, with a teacher who didn't want the job. Day five hundred eleven.

Mahapajapati Gotami comes to the Buddha again, this time with five hundred nuns, asking him to teach them. In the hundred and forty-sixth discourse, the senior monks have been taking turns teaching the nuns. It's the turn of an elder named Nandaka, and he doesn't want to go. Nobody says why. The Buddha asks Ananda whose turn it is, hears the answer, and turns to Nandaka himself: teach the nuns, Nandaka. Give them a talk on the teaching. So Nandaka goes. Today: Nandaka's full moon.
screen: `FIVE HUNDRED NUNS ASK TO BE TAUGHT.` → `IT'S NANDAKA'S TURN.` → `HE DOESN'T WANT TO GO.`

segments.voice: He teaches by asking. Sisters, he says, is the eye permanent or impermanent? Impermanent, venerable sir. And what's impermanent, is it pain or ease? Pain, venerable sir. Is it fit to be called mine, me, my self? No, venerable sir. Through all six senses, and their objects, and their kinds of knowing. Then three pictures. An oil lamp is burning: the oil, the wick and the flame all change. Would anyone say its light stays the same forever? A great tree: its roots, trunk, branches and leaves all change. Would its shadow be permanent? And a skilled butcher with a sharp knife, separating the hide from the flesh without cutting either: that's wisdom, slicing cleanly through what binds the mind. The nuns are pleased. But the Buddha sees something. They're glad, he says, but not yet fulfilled. Teach them again tomorrow, Nandaka, the same way. So he does. And then the Buddha uses the moon to describe the difference. On the fourteenth night, nobody looking up has any doubt: the moon isn't full yet. It's close, but not full. That was the nuns after the first talk. On the fifteenth, nobody doubts either. The moon is full. That's the nuns after the second. The text says that the least of the five hundred had entered the stream. Look back at the week: many names for a bowl, a stranger in a potter's shed, the truths expounded, a robe made by hand, a dying giver, Punna going west. And now a reluctant teacher, sent back a second time, until the moon was full.
screen: `TEACHING BY QUESTIONS` · `A LAMP, A TREE, A SHARP KNIFE` · `GLAD, BUT NOT YET FULFILLED` · `THE FOURTEENTH, THEN THE FIFTEENTH` · then, large: `THE MOON IS FULL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: teach one thing kindly. Sit and settle. Think of one small thing you know well, how to make rice, how to calm down before a call, one line from this path. Picture someone who'd benefit. Picture teaching it the way Nandaka did: asking, not lecturing, and willing to say it again tomorrow if it hasn't landed. Then let the picture go, and rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Nandaka's full moon. A reluctant elder teaches the nuns twice, and they go from nearly full, like the fourteenth night, to full, like the fifteenth. Today's word.
Your line: the moon is full. Today, if you explain something and it doesn't land, try once more, kindly, the same way, and let it fill in. Day five hundred eleven.

oil, wick and flame all change

myth: Nandaka is eager to teach the nuns
he doesn't want to go; the Buddha himself asks him to teach.
after the first talk, the nuns are glad but not yet fulfilled
the Buddha sends Nandaka back to teach them again the next day.
Nandaka teaches mostly by asking the nuns questions
is the eye permanent or impermanent? is it fit to be called mine?

fork.setup: you're the Buddha. the nuns are pleased with Nandaka's talk, but you see they aren't yet fulfilled. what do you do?
options: teach them yourself instead.
send Nandaka back to teach the same way tomorrow.
tell the nuns to study on their own.
fork.reveal: Nandaka teaches again in the same way, and the nuns become like the moon on the fifteenth: full.

original.note: Pali punna: full. the moon of the fifteenth is full, and so are the nuns after the second talk.

trapdoor: what you thought: one good talk is enough.
what it means: the nuns were glad after the first and fulfilled after the second, like the moon going from nearly full to full.

what a scholar hears: MN 146, the Nandakovada Sutta, uses the uposatha moons of the fourteenth and fifteenth as its frame and states that the least of the five hundred bhikkhunis became a stream-enterer.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 146, Nandakovada Sutta (advice from Nandaka)
